author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
addressee: a congregation celebrating the feast of Saint Luke
occasion: A festal homily for the feast of Saint Luke the evangelist, praising his role as evangelist and physician and defending the mystery of Christ's birth from the Virgin.
argument: Hesychius opens by confessing his inadequacy yet speaking from love for the feast. He praises Luke as the evangelist who, by faith, beheld both the eternal generation of the Son and the incarnate mystery in the cave. He presents Luke as the physician chosen by Christ to heal humanity's varied spiritual diseases, and contrasts Luke's full account of the incarnation with the other evangelists. The homily then celebrates the Virgin Mary as the one who alone received the greeting 'Rejoice,' interpreting Isaiah's 'voice of crying' as a prophecy of the virginal birth, and closes with a brief account of Luke's life, writing, and death.

outline.move: The preacher confesses his inadequacy but speaks from love, and praises Luke as the evangelist who by faith beheld the eternal generation of the Son and the consubstantial Trinity.
Christ chose disciples from every trade, including Luke the physician, to heal humanity's spiritual diseases; Luke's Gospel is shown to be his medical art.
The other evangelists each told one part of the story, but Luke told the whole mystery of the incarnation, beginning with Gabriel's greeting to the Virgin.
The Virgin alone is worthy of the greeting 'Rejoice'; Isaiah's 'voice of crying' is interpreted as a prophecy of the virginal birth; the homily closes with Luke's life, writing, and death.

cast.name: Luke
cast.who: The evangelist and physician praised in the homily, companion of Paul and author of the Gospel.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle whom Luke accompanied until Paul's martyrdom.

cast.name: Mary
cast.who: The Virgin Mother of Christ, addressed as 'Rejoice, favored one.'

cast.name: Gabriel
cast.who: The angel who announced the conception to Mary.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: The prophet whose 'voice of crying' is interpreted as a prophecy of the virginal birth.

cast.name: Elizabeth
cast.who: The mother of John the Baptist, called 'the city' in the interpretation of Isaiah.

cast.name: John the Baptist
cast.who: Called 'the voice' (φωνήν) in the interpretation of Isaiah, with his leaping in the womb called 'the cry' (κραυγήν).

cast.name: Matthew
cast.who: The evangelist and former tax collector, who began his Gospel with the genealogy.

cast.name: Mark
cast.who: The evangelist who proclaimed the incarnate ministry of Jesus.

cast.name: John the Evangelist
cast.who: The evangelist called the 'evangelical eagle' and 'theological lyre,' who proclaimed the eternal generation and co-eternal existence of the Son.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle chosen from among the fishermen.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first man, robbed of immortality by the devil.

cast.name: Eve
cast.who: The first woman, who gave birth in sorrow.

cast.name: Sarah
cast.who: The matriarch who gave birth in pain.

cast.name: Rebecca
cast.who: The matriarch who gave birth in groaning.

cast.name: Hannah
cast.who: The mother of Samuel, who gave birth in tears.

voices.how_marked: introduced by 'the angel's annunciation to the Virgin, saying' (τοῦ ἀγγέλου εὐαγγελισμὸν πρὸς τὴν παρθένον εἰπόντος)

voices.speaker: Isaiah (quoted)
voices.how_marked: introduced by 'the prophet Isaiah cried out' (ὁ προφήτης Ἠσαΐας ... ἐβόα)

key_terms.sense: One who proclaims the good news of Christ; here especially Luke as author of a Gospel.
The hidden divine reality of the incarnation and eternal generation, revealed to faith.
God's saving plan enacted in Christ's incarnation and earthly life.
The begetting of the Son; used both for the eternal generation from the Father and the temporal birth from the Virgin.
The Virgin Mary, emphasizing her virginal conception and birth of Christ.
Physician; applied to Luke both as his profession and as a figure for his healing of souls through the Gospel.
Flesh; used in phrases like 'according to the flesh' for Christ's human descent and incarnation.
The divine Word, the Son of God, who became incarnate.
The Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity, whose coming upon Mary effected the conception.
The Trinity, one in essence and three in persons.
Of the same essence; used of the Trinity to affirm the Son's and Spirit's full divinity with the Father.
Person of the Trinity, distinct yet united in essence.
The self-emptying of the Son in taking the form of a servant.
The becoming human of the Son of God.
The festal assembly gathered to celebrate the saint's feast.

scripture: The author cites the Septuagint and uses its book names and Psalm numbering. Quotations should be identified by modern English Bible book names and, where applicable, modern chapter and verse; Psalms should follow the Septuagint numbering used by the author, with the Hebrew numbering noted if it differs.
uncertain: The precise date of the homily is not stated in the text.
The exact occasion beyond the feast of Saint Luke is not specified.
The authenticity of the attribution to Hesychius is marked as doubtful in the source.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul (quoted via Luke's Gospel)... the quotations are from Paul's letters (Ephesians 4:30 and John 5:23)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τούτοις λέγων· «Μὴ λυπεῖτε τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον», κἀκείνοις βοῶν· «Ὁ μὴ τιμῶν τὸν Υἱὸν οὐδὲ τὸν Πατέρα τιμᾷ»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The first quotation 'Do not grieve the Holy Spirit' is from Ephesians 4:30 (Paul), but the second 'The one who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father' is from John 5:23, spoken by Jesus in John's Gospel, not Paul.

_unresolved_facts.claim: John the Baptist... Called 'the voice' (φωνήν) in the interpretation of Isaiah, with his leaping in the womb called 'the cry' (κραυγήν)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: φωνὴν τὸν Ἰωάννην καλεῖ, κραυγὴν τὰ σκιρτήματα λέγει
_unresolved_facts.fix: John (the Baptist) is called 'the voice' (φωνήν), but the 'cry' (κραυγήν) refers to 'the leapings' (τὰ σκιρτήματα)—the leaping of the baby in Elizabeth's womb, not John's leaping specifically. The brief should say 'the leapings in the womb are called the cry.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Hannah... The mother of Samuel, who gave birth in tears
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text mentions Ἅννα but does not identify her as the mother of Samuel; this identification is an assumption not supported by the source text.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἰωάννης δὲ ὁ εὐαγγελικὸς ἀετός, ἡ θεολόγος λύρα
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source uses 'Ἰωάννης δὲ ὁ εὐαγγελικὸς ἀετός' (John the evangelical eagle), which distinguishes this John from John the Baptist also mentioned. The source form should include the epithet or context to distinguish from the Baptist.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-mid: 'beginning with Gabriel's greeting to the Virgin'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὅλον ὁμοῦ διηγήσατο τὸ μυστήριον, τοῦ Γαβριὴλ τὰ εὐαγγέλια, τῆς παρθένου τὴν εὐλάβειαν, τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος τὴν ἐπιφοίτησιν, τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ μορφήν, τὴν ἀπαθῆ κένωσιν τῆς θεότητος, τὸ ἄτρεπτον τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως καὶ ἀσύγχυτον, τῆς παρθενίας τὸ ἄσυλον, τῆς συλλήψεως τὸ αὐτοσχέδιον, τοῦ τόκου τὸ ἄφθορον, τὸν τοῦ ἀγγέλου εὐαγγελισμὸν πρὸς τὴν παρθένον εἰπόντος· «Χαῖρε, κεχαριτωμένη, ὁ κύριος μετὰ σοῦ.»
_unresolved_facts.fix: Luke's account includes Gabriel's annunciation, but also the Virgin's reverence, the Spirit's descent, God's form, the passionless kenosis, the unchangeable and unconfused incarnation, the inviolability of virginity, the spontaneous conception, and the incorruptible birth—not 'beginning with' Gabriel's greeting as a starting point but including it among many elements.

_unresolved_facts.claim: defending the mystery of Christ's birth from the Virgin
_unresolved_facts.fix: The homily celebrates and expounds the mystery of Christ's birth from the Virgin, but 'defending' implies apologetic or polemical purpose against specific objections, which is not the primary tone. The text is more encomiastic and catechetical than defensive.
